architecture.mechanism: Geothermal heat used as the drying energy source — applied heat drives moisture out of solid deposits (geothermal-assisted drying), so that water-laden scale can be dehydrated and destabilized rather than mechanically chipped.
architecture.intervention: During the 4-day annual outage, isolate the wellhead cyclone separators and flash vessel and run a geothermal-brine-heated drying cycle through the existing internals: circulate hot dry air or low-pressure steam tapped from the brine/flash system (kept below 180°C, no welding on the pressure boundary, on-site equipment only) to dehydrate the calcite and silica-gel deposits; the resulting shrinkage and cracking spalls the scale off the internals so it can be flushed/brushed clear, and the cycle is repeated each outage to keep scaling within serviceable limits.
architecture.expected_effect: Dehydration of the calcite and silica gel causes shrinkage, micro-cracking and detachment from separator walls and flash-vessel internals, restoring flow area and heat-transfer surface and recovering a substantial portion of the 6–11% quarterly thermal-output loss, with calcium tolerance to 900 mg/L unaffected since the mechanism is physical dewatering, not chemistry.
architecture.falsification_test: Take a removed or spare scaled internal from the cyclone/flash vessel, run the drying cycle (air at 150–180°C for 4–8 h) with an identical untreated control, and measure adherent scale mass, deposit thickness and detached-area fraction before/after; the mechanism is falsified if dried samples show <20% detachment or no cracking versus control, or if the dried scale re-adsorbs brine moisture and re-adheres on re-exposure.
